title: Guelph updates demolition control by-law citywide
subtitle: Development fee changes, a new paramedic station property purchase, and debate on vacant homes and property standards.
overview: Council approved a new demolition control by-law that designates the whole city as a demolition control area {{vote:m4}}. It raises the fine for demolishing without a permit to the legislated maximum of $50,000 per dwelling unit. It also defines demolition by removal of the main floor assembly and asks for building permit plans for a replacement building, with exemptions for unsafe buildings and capital works. Signs posted at demolition sites will now include the contractor's contact number.

Council approved changes to development application fees, effective April 1, 2024 {{vote:m3}}. After a closed session, it directed the Mayor and City Clerk to sign the purchase agreement for property for a new paramedic station {{vote:m2}}.

Much of the discussion was about vacant and neglected homes, which the demolition by-law does not cover. Staff said property standards updates for heritage properties are due in July, and that vacant property rules are scheduled for 2027. Residents concerned about neglected buildings should watch for the July report.

decisions.detail: Council received the discussion paper and approved a by-law designating the entire city as a demolition control area {{vote:m4}}.
Council approved the revised development application fees, effective April 1, 2024, and directed that the Development Applications Fee By-law be amended {{vote:m3}}.
Council directed the Mayor and City Clerk to sign the Agreement of Purchase and Sale for property for a new paramedic station {{vote:m2}}.

debate: A delegate welcomed the higher fine but argued the by-law misses demolition by neglect, since owners can leave buildings vacant instead of demolishing. The delegate called for a vacant property register, proactive inspections paid for by owners, and a vacancy tax.

Staff said demolition control under the Planning Act cannot require conditions on non-residential buildings or mandate deconstruction and recycling. Staff said they know of no other tool for cleared commercial sites, and one councillor raised the former hotel site as an example.

One councillor said the new definition of demolition could let owners gut a house and rebuild it from the inside without a permit, as long as the main floor assembly stays. Staff said the definition is stricter than in other municipalities and is clear for staff.

Several councillors asked about a registry or inspections for vacant homes. Staff said the July report covers heritage property standards, vacant property regulation is scheduled for 2027, and they would not commit to a further report before reviewing existing tools.
Staff said the word 'may' in the building permit plans condition allows for exemptions, such as unsafe buildings or provincial road projects.
